tagline: From runes to the Eddas — a three-stage diploma in reading the language of the sagas and the skaldic poets.
philosophy: Old Norse is the language of the Icelandic sagas, the Prose Edda, the Poetic Edda, and the skaldic corpus. It is a North Germanic language, cousin to Old English, with four cases, three genders, strong and weak nouns, and a verbal system that any student of German will recognize. We teach it as a language to be read with notes, not spoken. You will earn the right to sit down with Hávamál, Völuspá, and the sagas of the Icelanders — to read them in the original with a glossary and a grammar at your side.
duration_estimate: 4–8 months at one hour per day
method: Reading-led. Grammar introduced in context. Every lesson contains lines from the Eddas or the sagas. By the end of Stage 3 you will have read the opening stanzas of Hávamál and Völuspá.
prerequisites: None. A knowledge of German or Old English helps (the grammars are cousins) but is not required.

stages.name: The Sound and the Shape
stages.subtitle: The alphabet, the special letters, the umlauts; reading aloud before parsing.
learning_outcomes: Read aloud any printed Old Norse text with accurate reconstructed pronunciation (Old Icelandic, c. 1200 CE).
Recognize and produce the letters not found in modern English: þ (thorn), ð (eth), æ (ash), ǫ (o-ogonek).
Pronounce the vowels (long and short) and the consonant clusters (hr, hl, hn at word-start, retained from Proto-Germanic).
Hear and reproduce the pitch accent (inherited from Proto-Norse, though less prominent than in modern Swedish or Norwegian).

lessons.title: The Alphabet
lessons.content: Twenty-seven letters. The Latin alphabet plus þ, ð, æ, ǫ. Modern Icelandic editions normalize medieval spellings. Manuscripts use variant letters and abbreviations; we use the normalized forms.

lessons.title: Þ, Ð, Æ, Ǫ
lessons.content: Þ and ð (thorn and eth) = both the voiced and unvoiced th. Æ (ash) = the vowel in English 'cat.' Ǫ (o-ogonek, sometimes printed as ö with an ogonek tail) = a back rounded vowel between o and a, like the vowel in English 'caught.'

lessons.title: Vowels — Long and Short
lessons.content: Nine vowels: a, e, i, o, u, y, æ, ø, ǫ. Long vowels marked with acute accent in modern editions: á, é, í, ó, ú, ý, ǽ. Length is phonemic: mál (speech) versus mal (bag). Y = high front rounded, as in French tu or German ü. Ø = mid front rounded, as in French peu.

lessons.title: Diphthongs
lessons.content: Three diphthongs: au (as in English 'house'), ei (as in English 'bay'), ey (like ei but starting from ø). The diphthong ǫu appears in some words.

lessons.title: Consonants and Clusters
lessons.content: P, t, k unaspirated after s (like in English 'spin,' 'stop,' 'skill'). Hr, hl, hn at word-start = voiceless r, l, n (like Welsh ll). Double consonants pronounced long. Voiced and voiceless fricatives distinguished: f versus v, þ versus ð, s versus z (latter rare).

lessons.title: Stress
lessons.content: Almost always on the first syllable of the root, as in Old English and German. Prefixes do not take stress.

lessons.title: First Words
lessons.content: Maðr (man), kona (woman), skip (ship), hús (house), orð (word), land, konungr (king), goð (gods), saga. Practice pronunciation. Listen to audio recordings of modern Icelandic pronunciation of Old Norse (close approximation).

lessons.title: First Sentence
lessons.content: Gylfi konungr réð þar löndum er nú heitir Svíþjóð. — 'King Gylfi ruled over those lands which are now called Sweden.' The opening sentence of Gylfaginning (the first part of the Prose Edda). Read it aloud ten times.

checkpoint.title: Stage 1 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Twenty letters and letter-combinations to identify by audio; ten words read aloud and recorded; five short sentences read aloud; ten modern English words transliterated into Old Norse spelling. Pass mark: 85%.

stages.name: The Sentence
stages.subtitle: The four cases, three genders, strong and weak nouns, strong verbs, the suffixed article; parsing before translating.
learning_outcomes: Decline any strong or weak noun in all four cases and both numbers.
Recognize and decline the suffixed definite article (maðrinn, konunginn, landit).
Conjugate a strong verb (six ablaut classes) in the present and past indicative.
Translate simple sentences of the form Subject + Verb + Object with prepositional phrases and a genitive of possession.
Read one-hundred-word passages from the sagas with notes.

lessons.title: The Four Cases
lessons.content: Nominative (subject), accusative (direct object), genitive (possession), dative (indirect object, accompaniment, instrument, location). No separate instrumental case; it merged with the dative.

lessons.title: The Three Genders
lessons.content: Masculine, feminine, neuter. Gender is grammatical, not always natural (kona 'woman' is feminine, but barn 'child' is neuter, and maðr 'man' is masculine). Every noun has a gender; you must learn it.

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Masculine a-Stems
lessons.content: Armr (arm), dagr (day), hestr (horse). Nominative armr, accusative arm, genitive arms, dative armi. Plural: armar, arma, arma, ǫrmum (note the u-umlaut in the dative plural).

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Neuter a-Stems
lessons.content: Land, skip (ship), hús (house). Nominative and accusative identical in both numbers. Genitive singular -s, dative singular -i, nominative/accusative plural no ending or -∅, genitive plural -a, dative plural -um.

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Feminine ō-Stems
lessons.content: Kona (woman), saga (story), gjǫf (gift). Genitive singular -u, dative singular -u, nominative plural -ur, accusative plural -ur, genitive plural -a, dative plural -um.

lessons.title: Weak Nouns
lessons.content: Goði (chieftain), tunga (tongue), hjarta (heart). The -an declension as in Old English. Most forms end in -a or -an. Simpler than strong nouns.

lessons.title: The Suffixed Definite Article
lessons.content: Unique to North Germanic. The article is a suffix, not a separate word. Maðr (a man) → maðrinn (the man). Kona → konan. Land → landit. The suffix declines: maðrinn, manninn, mannsins, manninum.

lessons.title: Adjectives — Strong and Weak
lessons.content: Góðr (good). Strong when used predicatively or without article; weak after the suffixed article. Inn góði maðr (the good man — weak). Góðr maðr (a good man — strong).

lessons.title: The Present Indicative of Strong Verbs
lessons.content: Bera (to bear) — Class IV. Ek ber, þú berr, hann/hón/þat berr, vér berum, þér berið, þeir/þær/þau bera. The verb endings as in Old English and German.

lessons.title: The Past Indicative of Strong Verbs
lessons.content: Ek bar, þú bart, hann bar, vér bárum, þér báruð, þeir báru. Six ablaut classes inherited from Proto-Germanic. Each class has its own vowel pattern (bíta/beit/bitum/bitinn; brjóta/braut/brutum/brotinn).

lessons.title: Weak Verbs
lessons.content: Kalla (to call), telja (to tell). Past tense formed with dental suffix -að-, -ð-. Ek kallaða, þú kallaðir, hann kallaði.

lessons.title: The Verb Vera (To Be)
lessons.content: Ek em, þú ert, hann er, vér erum, þér eruð, þeir eru. Past: ek var, þú vart, hann var, vér várum. Irregular, essential.

lessons.title: Prepositions and Case Government
lessons.content: Í + accusative (motion into) or dative (location in). Á + accusative or dative. Með + dative (with). Til + genitive (to, towards). Frá + dative (from).

lessons.title: Reading: Snorri, Gylfaginning, Opening
lessons.content: The first paragraph of the Prose Edda. Gylfi konungr réð þar löndum... Seventy-five words, with full glosses. Clear, straightforward prose.

lessons.title: Reading: Egils saga, Chapter 1
lessons.content: Kveld-Úlfr hét maðr... — 'There was a man named Kveld-Ulf.' The opening of one of the greatest sagas. Simple syntax, vivid narrative.

checkpoint.title: Stage 2 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Written. Decline ten nouns with and without the suffixed article; conjugate five verbs; translate a seventy-five-word passage from Snorri or a saga; parse twenty inflected forms. Pass mark: 80%.

stages.name: The Reading
stages.subtitle: Hávamál and Völuspá, opening stanzas. The capstone.
learning_outcomes: Read and translate the opening stanzas of Hávamál (stanzas 1–10, the ethical maxims of the High One) with notes.
Read and translate the opening stanzas of Völuspá (stanzas 1–10, the creation of the world and the coming of the gods) with notes.
Recognize and parse the structures unique to Eddaic poetry (kennings, variation, fornyrðislag and ljóðaháttr meters).
Decline any i-stem or u-stem noun and recognize the preterite-present verbs.
Translate any passage of thirty or fewer words from a glossed Old Norse prose or verse text at sight.

lessons.title: i-Stem and u-Stem Nouns
lessons.content: Gestr (guest, i-stem), sonr (son, u-stem). Minor classes but common words. Dative plural gestum, sonum.

lessons.title: Preterite-Present Verbs
lessons.content: Verbs whose present tense looks like a past tense. Vita (to know): ek veit, þú veist, hann veit, vér vitum. Mega (to be able), eiga (to own), munu (shall), skulu (shall).

lessons.title: The Subjunctive
lessons.content: Present and past. Used in conditions, wishes, indirect speech, subordinate clauses. Often identical to indicative in plural forms; context distinguishes.

lessons.title: The Middle Voice
lessons.content: Formed with -sk suffix (reflexive or reciprocative). Kallask (to be called, to call oneself). Finnask (to be found, to find each other). Unique to North Germanic; does not exist in Old English.

lessons.title: Pronouns — Personal, Demonstrative, Relative
lessons.content: Ek, þú, hann/hón/þat, vér, þér, þeir/þær/þau. Demonstrative sjá/sú/þat (this), sá/sú/þat (that). Relative particle er (who, which, that).

lessons.title: Eddaic Meter — Fornyrðislag
lessons.content: The old story meter. Four-stress alliterative lines as in Old English, grouped in stanzas of varying length (usually eight lines). Used in heroic lays (Atlakviða, Hamðismál).

lessons.title: Eddaic Meter — Ljóðaháttr
lessons.content: The song meter. Six-line stanzas: two long alliterative lines, one short full line (with internal rhyme or heavy alliteration), two long lines, one short. Used in wisdom poetry (Hávamál, Grímnismál).

lessons.title: Kennings
lessons.content: Heiti-kenningar (poetic synonyms): jǫrð = fold = grund (earth). True kennings: benvǫllr (wound-field = shield), hjǫrþing (sword-assembly = battle). Skaldic poetry is drenched in them; Eddaic poetry uses them more sparingly.

lessons.title: Hávamál, Stanzas 1–3
lessons.content: Gáttir allar, / áðr gangi fram, / um skoðask skyli... — 'All doorways, before one goes forward, one should look about...' The opening maxims. Close reading and scansion.

lessons.title: Hávamál, Stanzas 4–7
lessons.content: Advice on hospitality, wariness, moderation. Deyr fé, / deyja frændr... — 'Cattle die, kinsmen die...' The most famous stanza (76–77, but taught here for thematic continuity). Old Norse ethics in compressed form.

lessons.title: Hávamál, Stanzas 8–10
lessons.content: More maxims on speech, drinking, and reputation. The voice of the poem: gnomic, practical, unsentimental.

lessons.title: Völuspá, Stanzas 1–3
lessons.content: Hljóðs bið ek allar / helgar kindir... — 'Silence I bid from all holy kindreds...' The prophetess speaks. The creation poem begins. Mythology and cosmology.

lessons.title: Völuspá, Stanzas 4–7
lessons.content: The creation of the world from Ymir's body. Ór Ymis holdi / var jǫrð of sköpuð... — 'From Ymir's flesh was the earth shaped...' The most vivid cosmogony in Germanic literature.

lessons.title: Völuspá, Stanzas 8–10
lessons.content: The gods create Ask and Embla, the first humans. Ǫnd þau né áttu, / óð þau né hǫfðu... — 'Spirit they had not, sense they had not...' Close reading of the mythological vocabulary.

lessons.title: Poetic Vocabulary and Archaisms
lessons.content: Eddaic poetry preserves old words not found in the prose sagas. Regin (gods), sigtíva (victory-gods = gods of battle), vé (shrine), vǫlva (prophetess), rǫk (fate, twilight). You learn to recognize the poetic register.

lessons.title: Sight Reading Practice
lessons.content: Five short passages (twenty to thirty words each) from other sagas (Njáls saga, Laxdæla saga, Grettis saga) and from Snorri's Prose Edda, with glosses but no grammatical notes. The student parses and translates at sight.

checkpoint.title: Stage 3 Capstone Examination
checkpoint.format: Written, three hours. Translate Hávamál stanzas 1–10 with notes. Translate Völuspá stanzas 1–10 with notes. Scan and parse two stanzas (one fornyrðislag, one ljóðaháttr). Translate one thirty-word sight passage from a glossed saga text. Parse fifteen inflected forms. Pass mark: 70%. Honors: 85%.

certification.credential_name: The Kalopaideia Diploma in Reading Old Norse
certification.credential_subtitle: An attestation that the bearer has completed the three-stage course and passed the capstone examination.
certification.what_it_is: A privately-issued certificate of completion. Not an academic degree. Not a teaching license. It says: this person sat down with the Eddas and the sagas and earned an honest reading of them.
certification.what_is_recorded: Student's chosen public name; the language; the date of the capstone examination; the result (Pass or Pass with Honors); the SHA-256 hash of the student's signed examination scripts.
certification.what_is_not_recorded: The actual examination answers; the student's email or other identifiers; anything that could identify the student against their will. The certificate is pseudonymous if the student wishes.
certification.issuance: On-chain on Base as an ERC-721 soulbound (non-transferable) token. One certificate per student per language. The contract is owned by Kalopaideia and the minting key is held by the proprietor. The token URI points to a permanent, IPFS-pinned JSON document signed by Kalopaideia's issuing key.
certification.verification: Any third party can verify a certificate at kalopaideia.com/verify/<token-id> by entering the token ID and the certificate hash. The page will display the issuance date, the language, and the result.
certification.cost: Included in the Akousma subscription. The on-chain gas fee at issuance is paid by Kalopaideia. The student pays nothing extra.
certification.renewability: None. A diploma is not a driver's license. Once earned, it stands.
